On the local bus from Nashik Road to their kasba, Wasim was loud as usual. "That new singer from the TV contest, the one with the long braid? Total fake. Can't sing, just cries on stage. Everyone knows that."
Devika, squeezed next to the window, turned sharply. "I voted for her. Twice."
"Come on. Seriously?"
"My whole family watches for her. She sings old Marathi songs properly."
Suresh, from the seat behind, added, "My mother likes her too."
Wasim felt his neck go warm. "Why is everyone jumping on me? I'm just saying what's true."
"You're saying what you think," Devika said. "That's different."
He stared out at the sugarcane fields for the rest of the ride, not sure whether he was angry or embarrassed.

qa.q: How many times did Devika vote for the singer?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why does Wasim feel everyone is jumping on him?
qa.a: Wasim feels defensive because he believed his opinion was simply the truth everyone shared, so hearing others disagree felt like an attack rather than a normal difference.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he wants to share a strong opinion?
qa.a: Say it as his own view, like "I don't enjoy her singing", and ask what others think before calling it a fact.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt hearing her favourite singer called a fake?
qa.a: She might feel stung, since the singer means something to her whole family, so she pushed back.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy assuming everyone shares his view of a TV singer, speaking bluntly, and feeling attacked by disagreement.

In the corridor of their school in Madrid, Santiago slammed his locker. "Señora Ruiz is the worst teacher this school has ever had. She makes us act out every scene. It's embarrassing." He looked round, waiting for nods.
Kofi shifted his bag. "I actually like her class. It's the only one where I talk."
"You're joking."
"No. And Lucía said drama is her favourite subject."
Santiago felt heat rise up his neck. He had been so sure everyone groaned the way he did. "Great, so you're all on her side."
"It's not sides," Kofi said. "You just hate acting. That's fine."
Santiago walked to maths alone, going over it. He'd said "everyone" as if it were obvious. Maybe it had only been obvious to him.

qa.q: What does Señora Ruiz make the class do?
qa.a: Act out every scene.

qa.q: What does the heat rising up Santiago's neck suggest?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and a bit defensive, because he had been sure everyone felt the way he did.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Santiago try next time?
qa.a: He presented his dislike as everyone's view; next time he could say he finds her class embarrassing and ask how others find it.

qa.q: What is Señora Ruiz's class like for Kofi?
qa.a: It's the only class where Kofi talks, so it matters to him, which is why he gently disagrees.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy assuming his friends share his view of a teacher, speaking bluntly, and feeling ganged up on when they don't.

In the school bus bay after the Wednesday assembly, Anirudh, fifteen, dropped his bag on the bench. "That new sports teacher is useless. Can't even blow a whistle properly. Everyone thinks so."
Lakshmi looked up from her phone. "I don't. She fixed my running start in two days."
"Come on, Lakshmi. She's so slow. Sangeeta, tell her."
Sangeeta shook her head. "I like her. She lets us choose teams instead of always the captains."
Anirudh's face went hot. "Wow. Okay. So now I'm the bad guy?"
"Nobody said that," Lakshmi said.
"You're both ganging up on me." He pulled his earphones in and turned toward the window, still sure that most of the class agreed with him and these two were just being difficult.

passage: Last term I made a fool of myself over Mr Kulkarni, our new physics teacher. I'm Akash, and I found him boring: he wrote everything on the board and never told jokes. I was sure the whole of 10C felt the same, because my two closest friends did. So at lunch, in front of eight people, I said loudly, "Kulkarni is the worst teacher this school has ever hired." I waited for laughs. Instead Disha put down her roti and said he was the first teacher who had ever made current electricity make sense to her. Three others nodded. My face burned and I snapped that they were just sucking up. Walking home, I realised I had only ever asked two people. That's not a whole class.

qa.q: What did Disha say about Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: Disha said he was the first teacher who had ever made current electricity make sense to her.

qa.q: Why did Akash snap at the others when they disagreed?
qa.a: Akash felt embarrassed and attacked, having been so sure the whole class agreed that a different view felt like a personal challenge.

qa.q: What could Akash do before sharing a strong opinion with a group?
qa.a: Akash could ask a few people what they think first, and remember that two close friends aren't the whole class.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Mr Kulkarni was called the worst teacher?
qa.a: Disha probably felt uncomfortable, but brave enough to defend a teacher who had helped her understand physics.

grounding: Shows a teenager assuming the whole class shares an opinion of a teacher, saying it bluntly, then feeling attacked when others disagree.

passage:
Drama club supervisor's note, 9 February.
During the break Abhinav put on a clip of a pop singer everyone's been talking about and started mimicking her dance, calling it "the cringiest thing on earth, right, guys?" He clearly expected the room to laugh with him. Swati said, "I actually love her songs," and two others agreed. Abhinav went red. "You're joking. Nobody likes that." When they kept disagreeing, he packed his bag and said everyone was ganging up on him. I asked him to stay back. We talked about how many people he had actually asked before deciding that everyone agreed. He admitted it was his cousin and one friend. I suggested he try asking "what do you think?" before announcing. He rolled his eyes, but he nodded.

qa.q: What did Abhinav call the pop singer's dance?
qa.a: He called it 'the cringiest thing on earth'.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav feel ganged up on?
qa.a: Abhinav felt embarrassed and attacked, because he truly expected the whole room to share his opinion, so disagreement felt like people turning on him.

qa.q: What small step did the supervisor suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: The supervisor suggested asking 'what do you think?' before announcing, which lets Abhinav find out real opinions instead of assuming them.

qa.q: What might it have taken for Swati to speak up about loving the songs?
qa.a: Swati had to disagree with a loud, confident person in front of others, which can feel risky, so it took some courage.

grounding: Shows a teenager assuming everyone shares his opinion of a singer, speaking bluntly, and feeling ganged up on when others disagree.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
Can't sleep. Tonight I posted in the class group that the new PT sir is "a total dictator" for making us run laps in the heat. I honestly thought everyone would agree. We all complain on the field! Within ten minutes Rajni wrote that he's the only teacher who ever picked the shy kids for the relay, and five people liked that message. Five. Nobody liked mine. Maybe complaining on the field isn't the same as agreeing with me. Maybe they were just tired. Tomorrow I'll say sorry to Rajni. Not sure about PT sir yet.

So, Lalremsiami, you wanted a story for the podcast about getting things wrong. I'm Eshaan, and this one still makes me cringe.
Our football team got a new coach last term. I thought she was far too strict: laps, no phones, practice at six. In my head, the whole team hated her. The guys I travelled with complained every single day.
So at the team meeting, when she asked for feedback, I stood up and said, "Honestly, all of us think your rules are ridiculous."
Silence. Then our goalkeeper said, "Speak for yourself. I've never played better." Two others nodded. The captain said the six o'clock practice was the best thing that had happened to us.
I felt like I'd been punched. I sat there thinking, they're all against me. It took me a week to see it. I'd only ever asked the three people in my auto.

qa.q: What time was practice under the new coach?
qa.a: Practice was at six.

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel when the goalkeeper disagreed?
qa.a: Eshaan felt shocked and attacked, as if punched, having been sure the whole team agreed.

qa.q: What could Eshaan have done before speaking for the team?
qa.a: Eshaan could have asked more teammates first, or given feedback as a personal view, since only the three people in the auto had been asked.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt when Eshaan said 'all of us'?
qa.a: The coach may have felt hurt or defensive at first, then reassured when the goalkeeper and captain spoke up.
